A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same topologically regularized MIL research. All 11 pages of v1 and 14 pages of v2 support comparison, including v2 Appendix A.1–A.3; v1 has no appendix. The losses, anemia cohort, tables, and reused figures can be matched despite substantial expansion and rewriting.

before.justification: Section 4 and Table 1 report original anemia-classification experiments with repeated-run results. Figures 1, 4, and 5 provide learning curves and instance-level analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains the anemia experiments and adds original toy, standard MIL benchmark, and synthetic-dataset results, including analyses in Appendix A.2–A.3.

M1.justification: V2 adds an implemented regressor-guided pooling variant, TR-RGMIL, extending the framework's aggregation options (Appendix A.1). The central procedure remains unchanged: zero-dimensional persistent homology, bidirectional distance-matching regularization, and its weighted addition to classification loss. The anemia dual-head loss is retained in Appendix Eq. 17.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only the five-class anemia cohort. V2 retains this coverage and adds MUSK1/MUSK2 molecular-conformation tasks, FOX/TIGER/ELEPHANT image-feature benchmarks, bagged MNIST and Fashion-MNIST classification, and a 100-dimensional hypersphere toy task.

E2.justification: The original four anemia pooling comparisons remain. V2 adds RGMIL as a reimplemented comparator and standard attention pooling in synthetic experiments. Its benchmark Table 1 also compares against published APMIL, GAPMIL, DPMIL, DSMIL, and BDRMIL results, explicitly distinguishing these literature scores from reimplemented results.

E3.justification: V2 introduces ten-fold benchmark evaluation and synthetic protocols varying training budgets from 10 to 200 bags and Gaussian bag sizes with means 10, 50, and 100. Anemia evaluation adds precision and recall while retaining three-fold evaluation. The anemia image total changes from 3630 in v1's body to 521, already stated in v1's abstract; this inconsistent description does not establish a reduced dataset.

E4.justification: V2 adds a toy latent-representation case study, training-data and bag-size sensitivity analyses, and synthetic/benchmark learning curves (Figures 2–4, 7–8). V1's anemia learning curves in Figure 1 are removed. Its anomaly-score and distance-heatmap analyses remain as v2 Figures 5–6 and are not new analyses.

E5.justification: The anemia table retains its three-fold, three-run mean-and-standard-deviation reporting. V2 adds five-run reporting for new experiments; Figure 3 pools five runs across three bag sizes, totaling 15 runs. This adds repetition and aggregation information without establishing increased replication of the retained anemia experiments.

E6.justification: V1 Table 1's accuracy, F1, and AUROC values and deviations are unchanged in v2 Table 2; regularized average-pooling accuracy remains 81.29 ± 2.5. V2 adds precision/recall entries and extensive benchmark, toy, and synthetic results, including TR-RGMIL's 0.970 ± 0.042 on MUSK2. These are additional results, not improvements over v1 under retained settings.

T1.justification: Section 4 adds computational-complexity reasoning that pairwise-distance construction dominates zero-dimensional signature calculation at O(n²), together with a parameter-count argument. The principal loss equations remain equivalent. Expanded descriptions of Vietoris–Rips filtrations and existing pooling formulas do not constitute a new theoretical framework or proof.

C1.justification: The contribution expands from anemia classification with a claimed improvement exceeding 3% to a general MIL solution for data scarcity across aggregation strategies and domains. V2's abstract introduces average improvement claims of 2.8% for benchmarks, 15.3% for synthetic datasets, and 5.5% for biomedical data, although the original anemia scores remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretations of latent structure, scarce-data generalization, and differences between aggregation functions. It adds a rationale favoring topological over direct distance-preservation loss, including noise-robustness and scale-invariance claims without a corresponding new comparison experiment. V1's caveat about average pooling's weaker medical interpretability is omitted, while variance-reduction language becomes qualified as occurring often.

D1.justification: Appendix Tables 3–6 add extensive architecture, optimizer, epoch-budget, and early-stopping details, including newly disclosed anemia settings. Conversely, v1's precise auxiliary-loss decay, five-epoch GMM-refitting schedule, and A100/228-hour resource disclosure disappear. Synthetic regularization weights are deferred to source code without an access link, and several architecture dimensions conflict with the described inputs or tasks.

R1.justification: V2 adds a substantial related-work section positioning the method against general MIL aggregation approaches, particularly Du et al.'s RGMIL and its limitations under data scarcity. Citations and discussion expand to additional attention, pooling, biomedical, and topology research. This materially broadens the earlier anemia-centered research positioning.

P1.justification: The title, author list, abstract, introduction, and substantial portions of the methods and discussion are rewritten. The narrative becomes a general data-scarcity study with separate related work, dataset-specific experimental subsections, an impact statement, and technical appendices. Existing auxiliary-loss material moves into Appendix A.1.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main text to a two-column layout and redraws the framework schematic, incorporating the persistent-homology illustration. It adds benchmark and architecture tables and multiple experimental plots. The anemia table is enlarged with two metric rows, while the retained cell and heatmap figures are resized, relabeled, and relocated.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important evidential limitation: v1 supported its data-scarcity argument using one anemia cohort, whereas v2 directly investigates training budgets and bag sizes across additional domains. These controlled analyses substantially strengthen the central empirical argument while retaining the original clinical findings. Missing synthetic regularization weights, inconsistent appendix dimensions, and the unclear basis of the revised 5.5% anemia headline weaken reporting, but the targeted validation gains outweigh these shortcomings.
